title: Everybody Wants an AI Supercomputer. Nobody Wants to Pay the Electric Bill.
dek: The semiconductor industry has a new problem. Building faster chips was the easy part. Feeding them, cooling them, and keeping them busy is getting expensive.
body: Somebody asked me recently what the most important component in an AI data center is.
I said the electrical connection.
He thought I was joking.
Look, NVIDIA can build extraordinary processors. AMD can build extraordinary processors. The memory companies are doing some remarkable work, too.
But none of those chips accomplishes much if you can't deliver enough electricity to the building, remove the heat, and keep the processors supplied with data.
That's where the conversation gets interesting.
We've spent years talking about how many calculations a GPU can perform. Now we're building machines where the processor is only one part of a much larger engineering problem.
## The rack is becoming the computer
Take NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 architecture.
Instead of thinking about individual accelerator cards, think about an entire rack operating as a tightly interconnected computing system.
The design combines 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs using a high-bandwidth NVLink fabric.
That's a very different proposition from buying a handful of GPUs and putting them into ordinary servers.
You're buying the processors, interconnect, memory architecture, power distribution, cooling system, and a substantial amount of supporting infrastructure.
And all those components have to work together.
A processor can have spectacular theoretical throughput and still spend an embarrassing amount of time waiting for data.

That's why memory bandwidth matters. That's why communication between accelerators matters. And that's why the physical design of these systems is becoming inseparable from their computational performance.
## The memory problem isn't going away
Large AI models move enormous quantities of data.

During inference, the system repeatedly accesses model weights and attention-related data. Depending on the workload, memory bandwidth and capacity can become more important constraints than raw arithmetic throughput.
High-bandwidth memory helps address that problem, but it introduces its own engineering and manufacturing challenges.
You need advanced packaging. You need memory stacks close to the processor. You need adequate yields. You need the entire supply chain working at the same time.
You can't solve a memory bottleneck by simply advertising more floating-point operations.
And when a model is distributed across multiple accelerators, communication becomes another constraint.
The interesting number isn't necessarily how quickly one chip can multiply matrices.
It's how much useful work the entire system completes while meeting the application's latency requirements.
## Then there's the heat
Let's talk about something less glamorous.
Cooling.
When you pack high-performance processors into dense racks, you create an enormous thermal-management problem.
Air cooling becomes increasingly difficult at these densities, which is why liquid cooling has become central to advanced rack-scale AI systems.
But liquid cooling isn't just a matter of running some pipes behind the servers.
You have pumps, heat exchangers, coolant distribution units, leak detection, maintenance requirements, and facility-level engineering decisions.
The data center itself becomes part of the computing architecture.
And if the cooling system fails, it doesn't matter how impressive the accelerator specifications are.
## What a data center actually costs
Here's a hypothetical example.
Suppose a facility operates a continuous 10-megawatt IT load.
At 8,760 hours per year, that's 87.6 million kilowatt-hours annually for the computing equipment alone.
At an illustrative electricity price of ten cents per kilowatt-hour, the annual IT electricity bill is $8.76 million.
Now assume a power usage effectiveness, or PUE, of 1.2.
The total facility consumes approximately 105.12 million kilowatt-hours annually, bringing the electricity cost to roughly $10.51 million.
That's before hardware purchases, networking, land, construction, financing, maintenance, and staffing.
And ten megawatts is not an especially large number in the context of ambitious AI infrastructure development.
The arithmetic is straightforward. The actual economics aren't.
Electricity prices vary by location and contract. Utilization varies. Cooling designs differ. Hardware depreciates. Grid connections can take time to secure.
A cheap processor in an expensive facility may not be a cheap computing system.
## The question I'd ask NVIDIA
I wouldn't start by asking how much faster the next GPU is.
I'd ask how much useful inference work a complete installation delivers per megawatt, at a specified latency, under sustained production load.
Then I'd ask the same question about training throughput.
And I'd want to know what happens when you include networking overhead, memory constraints, failures, maintenance, and idle capacity.
Those measurements are considerably harder to put on a marketing slide.
They're also the numbers that matter when somebody is deciding whether to spend hundreds of millions of dollars building infrastructure.
## The next semiconductor competition
NVIDIA's advantage isn't simply that it makes fast GPUs.
It's the surrounding ecosystem: software, networking, systems integration, developer tools, and the ability to deliver a computing platform rather than an isolated chip.
AMD and other competitors don't necessarily have to beat NVIDIA on every specification to win business.
They have to offer a sufficiently attractive combination of performance, software compatibility, availability, power efficiency, and total cost.
And customers have to believe the systems will work reliably at scale.
That's the real competition.
Not who can put the largest number on a slide.
Who can deliver the most useful computing capacity, keep it running, and make the economics work?
Because the electricity company doesn't care whose logo is on the GPU.
It sends the bill either way.

Editorial note: The 10-megawatt facility calculation uses hypothetical electricity pricing and PUE assumptions. This is technical analysis, not a claim about a particular data center's operating expenses.
